title: Lab 6 – Hyperaldosteronism, Cushing, pheochromocytoma
html:
Source: LP 6.pdf – 4 pages

Primary hyperaldosteronism- causes and screening #1

  • Etiology: bilateral idiopathic adrenal hyperplasia (60% of cases), aldosterone-producing
  • adenoma (35% of cases), aldosterone-producing adrenal carcinoma
  • Screening indications:
  • - Patients resistant to conventional antihypertensive medication (not controlled on 3 agents)
  • - Patients with hypertension stage 2 or 3 (BP > 160–179/100–109 mmHg).
  • - Hypertension associated with hypokalemia (K<3.7 mmol/L, irrespective of thiazide use).
  • - Hypertension developing before the age of 40 years.
  • - Adrenal incidentaloma.
  • - Whenever considering secondary hypertension.
  • Primary hyperaldosteronism- diagnosis
  • A) Case-detection tests: aldosterone excess identification
  • 1. Electrolytes- ↑Na, ↑Cl, ↓ K
  • 2. Paired measurement (at 8-10 a.m.) of random plasma aldosterone concentration (PAC) and
  • plasma renin activity (PRA) (aldosterone: renin ratio = the case-detection test of choice).
  • !!A high PAC–PRA ratio (>20) and a PAC of at least 15 ng/dL are highly suggestive of primary
  • hyperaldosteronism.
  • - tests should be carried out in the normokalemic situation.
  • - medication that might interfere and that must be stopped (4 weeks prior to
  • diagnostic tests) includes mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (spironolactone,
  • eplerenone) and β-blockers (these medications can ↓ renin)
  • B) Confirmatory Tests- oral sodium loading, saline infusion, fludrocortisone suppression, and
  • Captopril challenge
  • An increased PAC–PRA ratio= NOT diagnostic by itself-> primary aldosteronism must be
  • confirmed by demonstrating lack of suppressibility of aldosterone secretion
  • C) Studies for detecting the lesion responsible for aldosterone excess
  •  Adrenal CT
  • Patients with confirmed primary aldosteronism should initially undergo imaging of the adrenal
  • glands with CT. It should be noted, however, that the frequency of adrenal incidentalomas
  • rises with age and, for this reason, it is prudent to consider adrenal venous sampling, if in
  • doubt.
  •  Adrenal Venous Sampling
  • Aldosterone measurements from both adrenal veins allow a gradient between the two sides
  • to be identified in the case of unilateral disease. It is the gold standard for differentiation
  • between unilateral and bilateral disease in patients with primary aldosteronism who want to
  • pursue surgical management for their hypertension.
  • !!The procedure should only be undertaken in patients in whom surgery= feasible and desired.

Primary hyperaldosteronism- treatment #2

  • Surgery: Unilateral laparoscopic adrenalectomy= the treatment of choice for unilateral
  • aldosterone-secreting adenoma (Conn’s syndrome)
  • Medical Therapy= treatment of choice for bilateral idiopathic hyperplasia. Also used: patients
  • with adenomas unlikely to be cured by surgery/ unfit for operation/who refuse surgery
  • -The MC receptor antagonist Spironolactone (50–400 mg/day; once daily administration) =
  • treatment of choice. BP and K should be monitored. Side effects: gynecomastia and impotence
  • in M, menstrual irregularities in F (antiandrogenic and antiprogesterone effects)
  • -Alternative: Eplerenone (50–200 mg/day; twice daily administration).
  • -Other antihypertensive drugs: Amiloride, ACEI, sartans, thiazide, calcium channel blockers.
  • Pheochromocytomas and paragangliomas
  • = neuroendocrine tumors
  • Should be suspected in patients with:
  • • Family history of MEN type 2, VHL type 2, neurofibromatosis
  • • Hypertension who are young
  • • Severe hypertension, resistant to treatment—paroxysmal or sustained.
  • • Hypertensive crisis during general anesthesia/surgery.
  • • Hypertension and suspicious symptoms (headaches, diaphoresis, palpitations, or
  • tachycardia, episodic anxiety, tremor, abdominal or chest pain
  • • Adrenal incidentalomas.
  • Pheochromocytomas and paragangliomas- clinical picture
  •  Sustained or episodic hypertension often resistant to conventional therapy (~200/120
  • mmHg), -> risk of complications: stroke, hypertensive encephalopathy, left ventricular
  • hypertrophy, heart failure
  •  Patients may also be normotensive or even hypotensive
  •  Orthostatic hypotension
  •  Palpitation, headaches, sweating= the characteristic triad
  •  Other signs and symptoms:
  •  Pallor or flushing, seizures, chest pain, dyspnea, weight loss
  •  Paresthesia, visual disturbance, anxiety
  •  Caused by hyperglycemia/ DM
  •  Manifestations of the associated genetic conditions: Von Recklinghausen (type 1)
  • Neurofibromatosis (NF-1 Gene), von Hippel-Lindau type 2, MEN2A, MEN2B.

Pheochromocytomas and paragangliomas- diagnosis #3

  • Biochemical testing- Catecholamine hypersecretion
  • • plasma free metanephrines (the most sensitive test for detection of catecholamine excess)
  • • urinary fractionated metanephrines (more specific)
  • ! If plasma metanephrines are borderline-> urinary metanephrines may be used for
  • confirmation-> still in a doubt-> clonidine suppression tests can be employed (distinguishing
  • patients with pheochromocytoma from normal subjects with elevated normetanephrine levels
  • in context of stress)
  • • serum chromogranin A- useful test to diagnose and monitor tumors (mostly
  • paragangliomas) that fail to secrete catecholamines or metanephrines.
  • Genetic Testing- should be done in particular in those with bilateral tumors, extra-adrenal
  • localization, malignant tumor, positive family history or a syndromic presentation.
  • Localization Studies
  • !! Employed only when there is clear biochemical evidence of a PCA/PGL.
  • • CT of the abdomen and pelvis ± the thorax (in search of a paraganglioma) = the first-choice
  • imaging modality because of its excellent spatial resolution.
  • • MRI of the abdomen and pelvis/skull- useful in the diagnosis of adrenal PCAs, skull base and
  • neck PGLs, and metastatic disease (bright hyperintense image on T2 is suggestive for PGL).
  • • Abdominal ultrasound: might be able to diagnose tumors > 3 cm in diameter
  • • Scintigraphy using 123I-MIBG- indicated in patients with metastatic PPGL detected by other
  • imaging modalities, to detect occult PGLs and to determine whether an adrenal mass is a
  • pheochromocytoma.
  • • Positron emission tomography (PET)→ in patients with occult tumors or metastatic disease.
  • Pheochromocytomas and paragangliomas- management
  • 1. Surgical resection= curative in the majority of patients
  • - Laparoscopic- small tumor, apparently benign
  • - Open resection- for large (>6 cm)/ invasive pheochromocytomas/ for most
  • paragangliomas, but laparoscopic resection can be performed for small, noninvasive
  • paragangliomas in surgically favorable locations.
  • !! Prior to surgery, patients should be reasonably normotensive on medication, with an
  • average blood pressure of ≤130/85 mmHg, without symptomatic orthostasis. They should
  • also be well hydrated.
  • 2. Medical treatment with antihypertensive medication= essential for inoperable patients
  • - Calcium channel blockers (Nicardipine, Amlodipine, Nifedipine) = first line medication
  • for these patients
  • - Other options: α blockers, sartans, ACE inhibitors, β blockers

! Perioperative Medical Management #4

  •  Preoperative blockade with α-adrenergic receptor blockers (first-choice class of drugs)-
  • e.g. Doxazosin 2–16 mg/day, orally, for at least 7–14 days preoperatively to prevent
  • perioperative cardiovascular complications.
  •  Calcium channel blockers- excellent antihypertensive agents for patients with
  • pheochromocytomas, often used to further improve blood pressure control in patients
  • already treated with α-adrenergic receptor blockers (e.g. Nicardipine 20–40 mg/8 h,
  • Amlodipine 10–20 mg/day, orally); useful especially for patients who develop severe
  • orthostatic hypotension with α-adrenergic receptor blockers.
  •  Preoperative coadministration of β-adrenergic receptor blockers (e.g., Propranolol,
  • Atenolol) is indicated to control tachycardia only after 3–4 days of α-adrenergic
  • receptor blockers administration (risk of hypertensive crisis due to unopposed
  • stimulation of α-adrenergic receptors)
